title: Who Is Vivek Ramaswamy? The Cincinnati-Born Biotech Billionaire Who Ran for President — and Is Now Two Days From a Bid to Become Ohio's First Indian-American Governor
excerpt: His parents came from Palakkad, Kerala — an engineer and a psychiatrist who raised a Hindu valedictorian in Cincinnati. He made a fortune buying shelved drug patents, wrote the book that launched the anti-woke movement, ran for president at 37 and was picked to co-run DOGE. On November 3, Ohio decides whether Vivek Ramaswamy becomes the first Hindu governor in American history.
body:
• Vivek Ramaswamy, 41, the Cincinnati-born son of immigrants from Palakkad, Kerala, is the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio. Ohioans vote on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and a win would make him Ohio's first Indian-American governor and the first Hindu governor in the United States.
  • Ramaswamy built his fortune in biotechnology: he founded Roivant Sciences in 2014 after a hedge-fund career, and Forbes estimated his net worth at $2.3 billion in September 2026.
  • His road to this race ran through the bestseller Woke, Inc., the anti-ESG firm Strive Asset Management, a 2024 presidential run that ended with a fourth-place finish in Iowa, and a brief designation to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which he left on Inauguration Day.
  • The race against Democrat Amy Acton, Ohio's former health director, is a genuine contest: a Suffolk University poll of 500 likely voters conducted October 21-26 put Acton at 48% and Ramaswamy at 44%, and the winner will be inaugurated on January 11, 2027.

Two days from now, Ohio will decide whether the most improbable biography in American politics gets its next chapter. Vivek Ramaswamy — hedge-fund partner at 29, biotech founder at 29, bestselling author at 35, presidential candidate at 37 — is the Republican nominee for governor of the state where he was born, facing Democrat Amy Acton, the physician who directed Ohio's health department in the first months of the Covid pandemic. Incumbent governor Mike DeWine is term-limited, Democrats have not won an Ohio governor's race since 2006, and Ballotpedia lists the contest as a battleground election, with The Cook Political Report rating it a toss-up. If Ramaswamy wins, he would become Ohio's first Indian-American governor and the first Hindu governor in the United States.

A Palakkad family, a Cincinnati childhood

Vivek Ganapathy Ramaswamy was born in Cincinnati on August 9, 1985, to parents from the Palakkad district of Kerala. His father, Vadakanchery Ganapathy Ramaswamy, is a graduate of the National Institute of Technology Calicut who worked as an engineer for General Electric; his mother, Geetha Ramaswamy, is a graduate of Mysore Medical College who worked as a geriatric psychiatrist for Merck and Schering-Plough. The family, Palakkad Iyers, had an ancestral agraharam home in Vadakkencherry, and Ramaswamy spent many summer vacations in India as a boy.

He was raised in Ohio in the Hindu faith of his parents — the family attended a Hindu temple in Dayton — and, according to Reuters, attended a Roman Catholic high school, Cincinnati's Jesuit-run St. Xavier, where he graduated as valedictorian in 2003. He was also a serious junior tennis player, ranked No. 48 in the Midwest in the under-16 regional rankings in 2001. Relatives say he is fluent in Tamil and understands Malayalam, and he is a vegetarian.

Harvard biology, Yale Law, Wall Street

Ramaswamy took a biology degree at Harvard in 2007, graduating summa cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa; his senior thesis, on the ethical questions raised by creating human-animal chimeras, won a Bowdoin Prize. He was president of the Harvard Political Union and performed libertarian-themed rap under the stage name "Da Vek."

https://x.com/VivekGRamaswamy/status/2116942900172861649

In 2007 he co-founded Campus Venture Network, a network linking student entrepreneurs with investors, and joined the hedge fund QVT Financial, where he became a partner co-managing its biotech portfolio. He has said his net worth was already around $15 million before he finished his law degree at Yale in 2013, where he befriended future vice president JD Vance and held a Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans.

Roivant: the fortune, and the flop inside it

In 2014 Ramaswamy founded Roivant Sciences — the "Roi" stands for return on investment — on a simple arbitrage: large pharmaceutical companies shelve promising drug candidates for reasons that have little to do with the science, so buy the patents cheaply, develop the drugs in focused subsidiaries (the "vants"), and keep the upside. SoftBank invested $1.1 billion in Roivant in 2017, and in 2019 Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma bought Roivant's stakes in five subsidiaries, a deal on which Ramaswamy made $175 million in capital gains.

The model's showcase was also its cautionary tale. Roivant's subsidiary Axovant bought intepirdine, a candidate Alzheimer's drug that had already failed four clinical trials at GlaxoSmithKline, for $5 million, raised hundreds of millions around it, and took it public in an IPO that briefly valued the company at almost $3 billion — with, at the time, eight employees. Ramaswamy appeared on the cover of Forbes in 2015 promising the highest return on investment ever attempted in the industry. In September 2017 intepirdine failed its large clinical trial, Axovant lost 75% of its value in a day, and pension funds were among the shareholders left holding the loss; Ramaswamy, whose stake sat in the parent company, was largely insulated. Roivant itself was never profitable during his tenure. He stepped down as chief executive in January 2021, stayed as executive chairman, and left the company in February 2023 to run for president, remaining one of its largest shareholders.

The anti-woke author

Ramaswamy's second career began with a book. Woke, Inc.: Inside Corporate America's Social Justice Scam (2021) argued that large companies had fused business with social and climate politics to the detriment of shareholders and democracy alike, and it made him a fixture of conservative media. Two more books followed in quick succession — Nation of Victims (2022) and Capitalist Punishment (2023) — before Truths: The Future of America First in 2024.

In 2022 he put the argument into practice, co-founding Columbus-based Strive Asset Management with his high-school friend Anson Frericks, backed by investors including Peter Thiel, JD Vance and Bill Ackman. Strive branded itself the anti-ESG alternative to BlackRock and Vanguard: own the shares, vote against the politics. One shadow from that period has followed him into this race — in August 2026 a federal judge declined to dismiss a whistleblower-retaliation lawsuit by a former Strive executive stemming from his tenure, allowing her claims to proceed without determining whether the securities-law violations she alleged occurred.

President, DOGE, and the road home

Ramaswamy declared for the presidency on February 21, 2023, loaned his campaign more than $15 million, and ran as the field's most aggressive debater — an avowed American nationalist who largely spared Donald Trump while attacking everyone else. He finished fourth in the Iowa caucuses on January 15, 2024, ended his campaign that night and endorsed Trump.

A week after the 2024 election, Trump named Ramaswamy and Elon Musk to lead the proposed Department of Government Efficiency. The appointment lasted, in practice, not at all: on Inauguration Day, January 20, 2025, Ramaswamy dropped out of DOGE to focus on running for governor of Ohio. He filed for the race on February 15, 2025, announced on February 24 with Trump's endorsement the same day, and in May 2025 received the Ohio Republican Party's endorsement — the earliest it had ever endorsed a non-incumbent for governor. In January 2026 he named Ohio Senate president Rob McColley as his running mate and won Governor DeWine's endorsement. On May 5, 2026, he won the Republican primary with 82.4% of the vote.

The Ohio campaign: property taxes and a conservative turn

Ramaswamy's platform is built on household economics. At the Columbus Metropolitan Club on October 14, he proposed rolling property taxes back to their levels at the end of the pandemic and capping their growth, with the state putting more money into schools to offset the local revenue — "Nobody would have designed the system this way from scratch," he said. Late in October he announced a Day 1 executive order to investigate localities where property taxes have doubled since the pandemic. He opposes Ohio's sales-tax breaks for data centers, wants to reinstate the death penalty for the most serious cases, and has promised lower electricity bills, stronger workforce development and an overhaul of the state's universities, which he first proposed consolidating and now says should share resources.

Campaigning alongside Trump at a Youngstown rally in October, reported by IANS, he pledged stricter immigration enforcement and an end to sanctuary-city policies in Ohio, and framed it in his own family's terms:

"And I say this as the proud son of legal immigrants to this country: your first act of entering this country cannot break the law."

— Vivek Ramaswamy, Youngstown rally, October 2026

At the same rally he promised, in IANS's reporting of his words, to be "the most conservative governor this state has ever seen in our history, because we deserve it."

A tight, bruising final week

For all the money and national attention — AP has noted he turned his name recognition and Trump alliance into a record fundraising haul — Ramaswamy goes into Election Day narrowly behind. The Suffolk University/USA TODAY Network Ohio poll conducted October 21-26 had Acton at 48%, Ramaswamy at 44% and Libertarian Don Kissick at 4%; the FiftyPlusOne average late last week put Acton at 48.2% to Ramaswamy's 45.2%.

The campaign has been described as heavily negative on both sides, and its ugliest episode has cut against Ramaswamy. In October his campaign aired an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother — who lost custody of her daughter in 1978, when Acton was 12 — urging voters not to trust her. Ramaswamy took responsibility for the ad and defended it, arguing Acton had misrepresented her past; Governor DeWine and Senator Jon Husted, both Republicans who had endorsed him, condemned it and distanced themselves. The Suffolk poll found 72% of likely voters had seen or heard about the ad, but fewer than 1% said it had moved them from Acton to Ramaswamy.

Why the diaspora is watching

Ramaswamy's candidacy puts two diaspora stories in one frame. He is the meritocracy narrative in person — the engineer-and-doctor immigrant household, the Harvard-Yale ascent, the billion-dollar company — and he campaigns openly as a Hindu in a party whose base is heavily Christian, describing his faith's monotheism as common ground with the voters he courts. He has also spoken to the anxieties Indian Americans bring to his movement from the other side: at Turning Point USA's AmericaFest, according to Reuters, he denounced a rising tide of racism on the political right, citing racial slurs directed at Second Lady Usha Vance, who was born in San Diego to Indian immigrants:

"If you believe in normalizing hatred towards any ethnic group: toward whites, towards Blacks, towards Hispanics, towards Jews, towards Indians, you have no place in the future of the conservative movement. Period."

— Vivek Ramaswamy, AmericaFest, via Reuters

On the policy question that touches the diaspora most directly, he has backed reforming the H-1B work-visa programme to select on merit rather than by lottery. His wife, Apoorva Ramaswamy (née Tewari), is a laryngologist whom he met at Yale — he in law, she in medicine; they married in 2015, have two sons and a daughter, and are raising their family in the Columbus area.

What happens next

Ohio polls close on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A Ramaswamy victory would make a 41-year-old who has never held elected office the state's first Indian-American and first billionaire governor, and the first Hindu governor anywhere in the United States, with inauguration set for January 11, 2027. A defeat would leave Acton as Ohio's first elected female governor — and leave Ramaswamy, still only 41, with the largest national profile of any Indian-American politician of his generation and an obvious question about what he does with it next.
image_caption: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, photographed in 2026. The Cincinnati-born biotech founder faces Democrat Amy Acton in the November 3, 2026, general election.
nri_angle: The son of Palakkad, Kerala immigrants — a GE engineer and a geriatric psychiatrist — Ramaswamy would be Ohio's first Indian-American governor and the first Hindu governor in US history; he campaigns on legal-immigration pride, has denounced anti-Indian racism on the right by name, and backs merit-based H-1B reform.
author: Diaspora Desk
